Task
In this programming assignment, you will design and implement a single-page website with specified functionality and formatting using only HTML, SCSS, and Javascript. The content of the website is up to you. For example, the subject can be a company/organization, a product, or a personal/portfolio page. This assignment will give you first-hand experience with HTML5 (e.g. header, canvas, video), CSS3/SASS (e.g. use of webfonts, animations, layout), and Javascript(ES5 or ES6).
Requirements
Your webpage will have to implement the features listed below. Note that the examples are only meant to illustrate the features. You do not have to make your webpage look similar to the examples. You just have to incorporate that feature in some form.

Layout: All content must be laid out in a single page with full-width horizontal stripes/sections including a header and a footer - Example

Sticky Navbar: A top navigation bar that sticks to the top of the window when scrolling - Example

Position Indicator: Indicator of the current reading position visible in the navigation bar (see above gif for example). Make sure your implementation highlights the last menu item when you scroll to the bottom of the page. ( Implementation Tip : To figure out which menu item to highlight, you’ll have to figure out which section lies directly below the bottom margin of the navigation bar. You can use methods that give you the height and position of different divs to figure that out. You will want to recompute this whenever there is a scroll event.)

Navbar Resizing: Navigation bar must be larger when users are at the top of the page. As users start scrolling down, it should resize and become smaller. Note that the text font size should also start larger and become smaller as users scroll down - Example

Smooth Scrolling: Smooth scrolling when navigating to a different section using the navigation bar - Example

Carousel: A section with a carousel/slider using a minimum of three slides. It should include the navigation arrows on the side - Example

Multi-column layout: A section with Multi-column content (3 or more columns) - Example

Centering: Content in each horizontal stripe/section must be horizontally centered. At least one element on the page must be vertically centered. The vertically-centered element should remain centered even if the dimensions of its outer element changes.

Responsiveness: Your webpage should look good when resized to the following resolutions:

1920x1080

1366x768

1280x720

1024x768

768x1024

Background Image: A section which uses a fixed-position background image - Example

Modal: A section which uses modal windows with additional content - Example

Video: Embedded video using HTML5 video tag - Example

SCSS features/CSS variables - You must utilize some SCSS features (e.g. variables, mixins, etc). A plain CSS file will receive less points.

CSS3 Animations: At least one use of CSS3 animations (e.g. fade in/out, transitions)

At least one use of scalable vector icons through CSS (e.g. FontAwesome)

Inclusion of social media icons

This is an individual assignment. No collaboration is permitted.

It is not permitted to copy/paste code that is not your own. You are, however, free to look at different code sources for inspiration and clarity. All sources (code as well as reading material) that you reference to complete this assignment must be declared in the submission.

No libraries are permitted (i.e. Bootstrap, JQuery, React, UIKit...etc.).

There should be no use of inline styling.

No inline script tags should be used.

HTML tables cannot be used for layout.

If you think something you’re doing might not be acceptable, please ask on Piazza.

Good diagnosis — you found the actual bug. Let's figure out why it caps at "stadiums" before fixing it.

Think about what rect.top <= navHeight actually means for the last section on the page. For every section except the last, there's another section below it — so once you scroll far enough, that next section's top edge slides up above the navbar, and the loop naturally advances currentIndex forward. But the very last section (video, or maybe your page ends with teams/video sitting tall) never gets "passed" by anything, because there's nothing after it whose rect.top triggers the condition for a later index — you just run out of page to scroll if the last section is shorter than one viewport height, or the browser simply can't scroll far enough for that section's top to be the "current" satisfying one relative to how the loop is structecd.

Actually — pause and check one thing first: is it capping at "stadiums" specifically because the page can't scroll further (i.e. window.scrollY maxes out before teams's or video's rect.top ever crosses the threshold), or is it a logic bug in the loop itself? If those two numbers are equal, the page has scrolled as far as it possibly can — meaning the content of your later sections is too short/empty to allow scrolling far enough for their tops to pass the navbar.

Done

That gap of exactly 100px is a good clue — and it happens to match the margin-top: 100px you added to header a few steps back to clear the fixed navbar. That's not a coincidence.

What's likely happening: margin collapsing. When a block element's first child has a top margin, and the parent has no padding/border to separate them, CSS "collapses" that margin — instead of pushing the child down inside the parent, the browser pushes the whole parent down and the margin effectively escapes to sit above the parent. Your <header> is the first element inside <body>, and body has no padding — so header's margin-top: 100px is collapsing through body and pushing body itself down, rather than staying "inside" the layout the way you'd expect.

This matters here because document.body.scrollHeight only measures body's own box — it doesn't account for that escaped, collapsed margin sitting above it. But the actual scrollable page height (document.documentElement.scrollHeight, i.e. the <html> element) does include it. That mismatch is your 100px discrepancy.

Two things to fix:

Re-run the check with document.documentElement.scrollHeight instead of document.body.scrollHeight, and see if the numbers match this time:

document.documentElement.scrollHeight - window.innerHeight

Compare that to window.scrollY at the bottom of the page.

Fix the underlying margin-collapse issue — swap header's margin-top: 100px for padding-top: 100px instead. Padding never collapses the way margin does, so it's the safer choice for this kind of "clear the fixed nav" spacing. Make that change in main.scss.

Try both, then re-check whether the two numbers from your original test now agree — that'll tell us whether "not enough scrollable content" is really the root cause of the teams/video highlighting issue, or if something else is going on.

Diagnosing an unexpected scrollbar despite matching width values.

That combination — scrollbar visible, but scrollWidth === clientWidth on every element you checked — is actually a strong sign the problem isn't your page at all. It's Firefox's Responsive Design Mode itself.

What's likely happening: RDM simulates a viewport of a given size (1920×1080) inside your actual browser window. If your real browser window isn't physically 1920px wide on your monitor, RDM has to render that simulated viewport at a shrunk zoom level to fit — and depending on the zoom/device-pixel-ratio settings, RDM sometimes shows its own scrollbars around the simulated device frame so you can pan around it, which is unrelated to whether your actual page content overflows.

How to check this theory:

In RDM, look for a zoom percentage dropdown near the top of the responsive design toolbar (often shows something like "100%" or "50%"). Try setting it to "Fit" or manually to 100% and see if the scrollbar behavior changes.

Alternatively, just resize your actual (non-RDM) browser window to be as wide as your monitor allows, and check for a scrollbar normally — no RDM simulation layer involved. If it's clean at real full width, RDM was the red herring.

Or check on an actual large external monitor / maximized window if you have one over 1920px wide.

Given your numbers all matched perfectly (no real overflow detected anywhere), I'd bet this is Recommendation #2 confirming there's no actual bug — but worth verifying directly rather than assuming. Try resizing your real browser window wide and let me know if the scrollbar persists outside of RDM.

(Note: & in HTML text must be written as & — that's why AT&T became AT&T, otherwise the browser tries to parse it as the start of a character entity.) SCSS — a map of city-name-to-filename, looped with @each: $city-images: ( 'mexico-city': 'mexico-city.jpg', 'guadalajara': 'guadalajara.jpg', 'monterrey': 'monterrey.jpg', 'toronto': 'toronto.jpg', 'vancouver': 'vancouver.jpg', 'nyc': 'nyc.jpg', 'boston': 'boston.jpg', 'philadelphia': 'philadelphia.jpg', 'atlanta': 'atlanta.jpg', 'miami': 'miami.jpg', 'kansas-city': 'kansas-city.jpg', 'dallas': 'dallas.jpg', 'houston': 'houston.jpg', 'la': 'la.jpg', 'sf': 'sf.jpg', 'seattle': 'seattle.jpg' ); .city-card { background-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.05); background-size: cover; background-position: center; border: 3px solid $border-color; padding: 24px; border-radius: 8px; color: $text-color; min-height: 200px; @each $name, $file in $city-images { &--#{$name} { background-image: linear-gradient(rgba(0,0,0,0.5), rgba(0,0,0,0.5)), url('../assets/cities/#{$file}'); } } } Walk through the new syntax: $city-images: (...) — this is a SCSS map, a key-value data structure (like a small dictionary). Keys are city slugs, values are filenames. @each $name, $file in $city-images — loops over every key-value pair in the map, binding $name and $file to each pair in turn. This runs inside .city-card's nesting, so it generates one &--slug { ... } block per map entry — 16 blocks from ~20 lines instead of writing all 16 by hand. #{$name} — this is string interpolation, needed because you can't concatenate a SCSS variable directly into a selector name or url() string; #{} tells SCSS "evaluate this variable and splice its value in as text here." Practically: drop your 16 stadium images into assets/cities/, named to match the map's values exactly (mexico-city.jpg, nyc.jpg, etc.) — if you'd rather name your files differently, just edit the map's values to match your actual filenames rather than renaming 16 files. Good — id="about" is back on <header>. But there's still a bug to catch in that same edit: document.querySelectorAll('header', 'section').

querySelectorAll only accepts a single selector string argument. The second argument you passed ('section') is silently ignored by the browser — it's not a valid parameter for this method at all. So this line is actually only selecting <header> elements, meaning sections right now is a NodeList containing just your one <header>, and none of your <section> elements are in it.

To select multiple tag types in one query, you combine them into a single comma-separated selector string:

const sections = document.querySelectorAll('header, section');

Note it's one string, 'header, section', not two separate arguments. This is standard CSS-selector syntax — the comma inside the string means "match either of these," which is exactly what a comma-separated list means in real CSS too (e.g. h2, h3 { ... } from your own stylesheet).

9/16/2026 19:47:39 Checking HTML structure, SCSS organization, and JavaScript patterns. Checking HTML structure, SCSS organization, and JavaScript patterns. Done Good moment to step back and audit against actual best practices, not just the assignment checklist. Here's a structured review across all three areas. HTML5 What's already solid: semantic tags (nav, header, section, footer), lang="en", alt text on real s, data-* attributes used correctly (not repurposing id/class), ; buttons get free keyboard support and the aria-label gives screen readers a real name instead of just "×". The modal itself has no ARIA role. Add role="dialog" and aria-modal="true" to #team-modal — this tells assistive tech "this is a modal dialog," which matters since visually it's obvious but programmatically it isn't without these hints. Not required by your assignment rubric, but it's the actual accessibility best practice for any modal. SASS/SCSS Already strong: variables, nesting, a data map + @each, string interpolation, a custom @function, a @mixin, %placeholder/@extend, nested media queries — genuinely broad feature coverage. Gaps worth fixing: Repeated magic number 1200px. You have $container-width: 1200px defined, but .about-image and video both hardcode max-width: 1200px directly instead of using $container-width. If you ever change the container width, these two won't follow — defeating the purpose of having a variable. Swap both to max-width: $container-width. Single monolithic file. At this size it's fine, but the standard-practice next step (mentionable in a write-up even if you don't do it) is splitting into partials — _variables.scss, _nav.scss, _carousel.scss, etc. — and combining them with @use/@forward (the modern replacement for @import, which Sass has deprecated). Not required for this assignment's scale, but worth knowing as the "correct" way to organize a larger Sass codebase. A few magic numbers without variables — min-height: 800px and max-height: 600px on the carousel, min-height: 200px on city cards. Not wrong, but a stricter best-practice reading would pull these into named variables ($carousel-height, etc.) alongside your existing spacing/font variables, for the same "change it once" reasoning as #1. JavaScript (ES6) Already solid: const/let only (no stray var), arrow functions, classList.toggle/add/remove instead of manual class-string manipulation, a for...of loop, template-free but clean string building. Gaps worth considering: No DOMContentLoaded guard. Your script queries the DOM (document.querySelector('nav'), etc.) immediately at the top level. This works only because your webpack setup loads main.js after the HTML is parsed — but that's an assumption baked into your build config, not something the script itself guarantees. Best practice is to not rely on load order and instead wrap your logic: document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => { // all your existing code }); This makes the script robust regardless of where or how it's loaded. 48 individual click listeners on team cards — one per .team-card, attached in a forEach. This works fine at 48 elements, but the more scalable pattern (worth knowing, not necessarily worth refactoring here) is event delegation: attach one listener to the parent .team-grid, and check event.target.closest('.team-card') inside it. That's one listener instead of 48, and it automatically covers any cards added later without re-binding. No null-checks on DOM lookups. document.getElementById('team-modal') etc. assume the element always exists. Fine for a project you control end-to-end and test yourself, but production code typically guards against a missing element (e.g. a typo'd id) causing a silent null.classList crash further down. None of the JS/SCSS gaps are things your rubric is checking for — they're "how would a working engineer critique this," which is a fair reading of your question. The

/
HTML gaps are the ones I'd actually prioritize fixing, since "semantic HTML5" is explicitly called out in your assignment description, and missing an

is the kind of thing a grader might specifically look for.
